BACTERIAL COELOMITIS EUTHANASIA. This 13-year-old female leopard gecko had not been eating on its own for several years and required assisted feeding. Recently the animal began to lose weight and was regurgitating after feeding. The animal was euthanized for humane and diagnostic purposes. At necropsy the animal was thin. There was abundant intracoelomic fat. The liver was enlarged. Multiple adhesions were between the intestinal organs with a large amount of inspissated material in the coelomic cavity.

ATRIAL RUPTURE MYOCARDIAL FIBROSIS RENAL ADENOMA CYSTIC ENDOMETRIAL HYPERPLASIA. This 13-year-old female warthog was sedated to move to a new enclosure. A tooth extraction was performed under sedation. The animal was slow to recover and was later found dead. At necropsy a large quantity of serosanguineous fluid was present in the pleura. A large blood clot was present in the pericardium arising from an atrial tear. A granuloma was noted in the liver. Cysts and edema were noted in the endometrium.

METASTATIC ADRENAL CARCINOMA EUTHANASIA. This approximately 26-year-old female sea lion was euthanized. It had a history of not eating well and had a chronic eye problem for several years. Physical exam revealed severe keratitis OU and mature cataracts OU. There was an intra-abdominal 12.5 x 10 cm. mass that was ovoid and firm. The mass was located medial to the right femur/pelvis. Suspect ovarian or renal associated tumor. At necropsy the abdominal and thoracic cavities contained copious amounts of transudative fluid. The lungs had multifocal pinpoint firm white plaques. The liver contained several 1-2 mm. white foci of normal consistency throughout the parenchyma. Lymph nodes were enlarged firm and necrotic. Ovaries were hard and white. There were areas of ulceration approximately 1 cm. in diameter within the lumen of the urinary bladder. Sections of abdominal lymph nodes have been frozen for future use if needed.

PANCREATITIS ISLET CELL DEGENERATION SEBACEOUS ADENOMA EUTHANASIA. This approximately 10-year-old male African hunting dog had difficulty ambulating and would not drink water. Euthanasia was performed for humane and diagnostic purposes. The animal had been on chronic low-dose steroids for several years due to allergy type dermatitis (G06-1602 G10-4932). This dog did not fully recover from anesthesia from the following day was ataxic especially in the real limbs and appeared to be tachypneic. Blood work revealed a stress leukogram hypertriglyceridemia elevated serum ALT and bilirubin and mild elevation in serum AST. Necropsy revealed nodules on the heart valves a 2 cm. focus of green discoloration in the right caudal pulmonary lobe and multiple firm lesions within the cranial aspect of the left pulmonary lobe. Some erosions were noted in the gastric mucosa and the pancreas was thickened discolored and possibly necrotic. The liver was congested and had a yellow tinge. The right kidney had a region of white discoloration on its serosal surface. The mucosal surface of the urinary bladder was erythematous and no urine was in the urinary bladder. Multiple white raised lesions were present along the abdominal fat.

Compartment 3: C3 Impaction Esophagus: Multifocal mucosal ulcers Peritoneal; thoracic; and pericardial cavities: Tricavitary effusion Liver: Hepatic lipidosis Subcutis of neck; dorsal thorax: Petechial hemorrhage Pericardium; endocardium; mediastinum: Petechial hemorrhage Lungs: Focal pulmonary consolidation Lip commissures: Bilateral proliferative dermatitis Comment The most striking gross findings were impacted ingesta in C3 and contraction of the aboral small intestine with nearly no intestinal content. The pathogenesis of this lesion is unknown. Negative energy balance likely contributed to hepatic lipid accumulation. The body cavitary effusions appeared transudative. Hemorrhages in the thorax and neck regions may represent terminal (agonal) changes. Lesions will be further evaluated histologically and ancillary testing for parasitology as well as bacterial cultures of the lung and liver are underway. The results of complete histologic evaluation and ancillary tests will be included in the final report. Charlotte Hollinger; VMD; MS; DACVP (Clinical Pathology) Lung: Mild multifocal suppurative bronchopneumonia with intralesional plant material Liver: Marked diffuse hepatic lipidosis and mild suppurative peridochitis Glandular stomach (C3): Small inestine: Mild lymphocytic and eosinophilic enteritis Skin: Moderate regional epidermal hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis with multifocal epidermal erosion; serocellular crusting; and mild superficial perivascular dermatitis C3 impaction with mild gastritis and enteritis; marked hepatic lipidosis; and perimortem aspiration pneumonia Comment The complete necropsy findings revealed C3 impaction; severe hepatic lipidosis; multifocal hemorrhage; and evidence of perimortem aspiration. A combination of factors likely contributed to the animals' illness; and perimortem aspiration may have contributed to worsening clinical picture and demise. The cutaneous lesions reported clinically consisted of proliferative epidermis with multifocal erosion and crusting. In addition to the clinically suspected differential of Orf (Contagious Ecthyma; Contagious Viral Pustular Dermatitis); another top differential is Idiopathic Nasal/Perioral Hyperkeratotic Dermatosis (also known as Munge); a relatively common condition in young alpacas and llamas for which the inciting cause is unknown. If desired based on herd or human health concerns; PCR testing for parapoxvirus (the inciting agent of Orf) could be pursued to further investigate the cutaneous lesion. Otherwise; this report concludes diagnostic testing in this case. Tissues will be retained for at least three weeks from the date of necropsy should further investigation be desired. INTESTINAL NEMATODIASIS BACTERIAL SEPSIS HEPATIC MELANOSIS. This 3.5-year-old male captive bred gecko was found dead with no prior signs of illness. The keepers had observed normal food and water consumption. Necropsy revealed adequate body condition but no discernible fat depots. The gastrointestinal tract was empty. The liver was firm on cut surface.

GASTRIC ULCERATION WITH HEMORRHAGE CESTODIASIS. This 2-year-old female mossy leaf-tailed gecko was found lethargic and off feed. Blood had been seen along the wall of the enclosure a few days earlier. Necropsy revealed good body condition and good postmortem condition. Internal organs were pale with the exception of the stomach that had a 0.5 cm. in diameter ulcer in the mucosa and a significant amount of fresh blood.

PULMONARY BACTERIAL GRANULOMATOSIS AND ULCERATIVE STAMATITIS. This 9-year-old python was found in agonal condition with blood coming from the mouth. The animal had a history of stomatitis and thin body condition. The snake died spontaneously. Necropsy revealed blood clots in the mouth and reddened mucous membranes. Blood clots were also detected in the stomach and small intestine.

EUTHANASIA DEGENERATIVE JOINT DISEASE. This 7-month-old female oryx was humanely euthanized. This calf was born with deviation of both hind limbs to the right side. It developed severe osteochondrosis dissecans of the right stifle and milder lesions in the left stifle. Despite arthroscopic surgery extensive chondroprotective and antifungal inflammatory medications and physical therapy there was no improvement. At necropsy there were foamy clear liquid flecks of ruminal fluid within the anterior portion of the trachea. There was mild congestion of blood vessels in the gastrointestinal tract and cerebrum. The thymus had petechiae. The right stifle had severe degenerative and erosive changes of articular cartilages particularly the lateral femoral condyle. There was a 0.5 x 1 x 1 cm. joint mass within the right stifle. The left stifle had moderate degenerative changes. The right coxofemoral joint contained blood tinged joint fluid. There was atrophy of the musculature of the right hind limb.

NEPHRITIS NEPHROSCLEROSIS RENAL TUBULAR NECROSIS BRONCHOINTERSTITIAL PNEUMONIA WITH SYNCYTIA EUTHANASIA. This 14.5-year-old male cougar had a history of chronic renal failure that had been managed clinically for the last few months. Euthanasia was performed for humane and diagnostic purposes. Necropsy revealed good body condition ample subcutaneous and coelomic fat stores pale yellow kidneys on cut surface a 2 cm. biliary cyst on the right hepatic lobe a few small cyst-like structures in the thyroid gland and no other gross abnormalities.

METASTATIC ADRENAL CORTICAL CARCINOMA UTERINE LEIOMYOSARCOMA SUBCUTANEOUS MYXOSARCOMA DEGENERATIVE CARDIAC AND RENAL DISEASE CAVITARY FIBROMATOSIS EUTHANASIA. This 20-year-old female lion was anesthetized two weeks earlier for inappetence lethargy and recent mane growth. Examination revealed subcutaneous masses in the right shoulder and right abdominal wall. Biopsy revealed benign epidermal and dermal hyperplastic changes and mixed perivascular inflammation. Fine needle aspirate revealed low nucleated cellularity with lipid material. Blood work revealed severe azotemia neutrophilic leukocytosis and mild anemia. Urinalysis revealed severe increase in urine protein/creatinine ratio proteinuria and glucosuria. Ultrasound identified decreased corticomedullary distinction and hypoechoic areas in the kidneys. A large mass-like structure was cranial to the left kidney and mild ascites was noted at the level of the urinary bladder. Supportive care was administered but inappetence persisted and the lion was euthanized for humane and diagnostic purposes. Necropsy revealed mane growth around the neck a 4 cm. subcutaneous mass in the right shoulder resembling a lipoma an 18 cm. mass compressing the esophagus and associated with both lungs fibrinous cavities with serous fluid within the mass multiple white firm nodules throughout the pulmonary parenchyma multiple mass-like structures adhered to the thoracic diaphragm fibrinous adhesions associated with masses in the diaphragm approximately 5 gal. of yellow-tinged free fluid in the abdominal cavity multiple cystic structures throughout the hepatic lobes a firm thickened small intestine yellow-tinged fluid throughout the gastrointestinal tract small amount of feces in the colon decreased cortical width in the kidneys a 22 cm. retroperitoneal mass next to the kidney and on cut surface the mass is friable and necrotic. A few 1-2 mm. cyst-like structures are in the uterus and mesentery. The mass appears to communicate with the uterus.

DEGENERATIVE CARDIOVASCULAR AND RENAL DISEASE. This 13.5-year-old female meerkat developed acute lameness of the hind limbs dragging the legs and associated dyspnea. A grade IV heart murmur was noted and no withdrawal reflex was noted in the legs which were probably cold. Euthanasia was performed for humane and diagnostic purposes. Necropsy revealed two foci of ischemia in the liver.

DROWNED. This 4-year-old male stork had been observed alive and behaving normally but was found dead in the river one hour later. Necropsy revealed water soaked but not water logged carcass good body condition and several yellow/green hard objects in the right axilla. The lungs were light pink and saturated with water. The heart was pale. The ingluvium and proventriculus are empty. Two bulges were found in the surface of the ventriculus one associated with the duodenal connection and one that was firm approximately 5 mm. in diameter and associated with several soft tissue pockets that contain firm black to brown fibrous matter. Ventricular incision revealed a small twig or thorn that penetrated full thickness through the ventriculus and ended in the second serosal bulge. The mucosal opening was fibrotic. The thyroids parathyroids and testicles were bilaterally enlarged (breeding season?). Brain case was intact and no luxations were found in the cervical spine.
HEPATITIS URATE STASIS MYOCARDIAL FIBROSIS. This 5-year-old bird was found dead. At necropsy the bird was thin. The liver was diffusely pale. Kidneys were pale tan.

EUTHANASIA INANITION SEMINOMA MYOCARDIAL FIBROSIS NEPHROSIS. This adult (approximately 9-year-old) male cockatiel was humanely euthanized. This bird had a history of glucosuria. It was drinking on average between 8-20 ml. of water daily. In late May it fell off its perch and remained recumbent. It was brought to the hospital and propped up in an incubator. Over the next few days his breathing became more labored and he was unable to support himself. At necropsy the bird was in thin body condition. The liver was small and slightly friable. The pancreas was light firm and enlarged.

EUTHANASIA PANCREATIC ISLET FIBROSIS DIABETES MELLITUS. This male 5-year-old hyrax was humanely euthanized for unresponsive diabetes mellitus. This is one of a larger group (family) that has been experiencing a case clustering of diabetes mellitus as a result of severe pancreatic islet fibrosis. This rock hyrax had elevations in amylase and lipase that supported an impending onset of diabetes mellitus. This past week the hyrax presented with diarrhea and off behavior. Urinalysis was profoundly glucosuric and blood work supported diabetes mellitus as well as renal failure. At necropsy the hyrax was in fair body condition. It had slight epaxial muscle atrophy indicating early weight loss. It also had a wet and soiled perineum from diarrhea antemortem. Both eyes had cataracts. A large swelling was found in the right femoral triangle that was associated with a 1 in. diameter hematoma presumed to be the result of venipuncture. Within the initial aorta and branches there was a Y-shaped plaque found on the intimal surface. Normal feces were apparent in the colon. The pancreas was firm on cut section but did not appear hyperemic. Yellow granulomas were located at the terminus of the spermatic cord. This hyrax was castrated at one year of age. Both kidneys were swollen and granular. Sections of liver spleen kidney and pancreas were frozen for future use if needed.

EUTHANASIA NONEPITHELIOTROPHIC LYMPHOMA. This 9-year-old female fennec fox had a history of neoplasia in the perineal and inguinal area. The lesion was previously diagnosed as nonepitheliotrophic lymphoma. The animal was humanely euthanized. At necropsy an erosion was noted in the articular cartilage of the shoulder joint and humeral head.

LOW-GRADE SEPSIS URATE STASIS. This 9-month-old python prolapsed its rectum one week prior to death and had not been doing well in the enclosure or eating prior to death. It was found dead in the enclosure. Necropsy revealed a necrotic tail tip full colon and no other abnormalities.

MYELOPROLIFERATIVE DISEASE. This 4.5-year-old female budgerigar presented in weak body condition with significant weight loss and loss of pectoral muscle mass. Supportive care was administered but the bird died overnight. Necropsy revealed a large solid mass in the right side of the coelomic cavity displacing the intestines to the left side. The mass did not appear to be connected to the kidney.

VISCERAL GOUT. This approximately 8-year/10-month-old female duck was one of a group of four whistling ducks found dead. At necropsy there were no signs of external trauma. The bird was mildly thin. The pericardium contained multifocal small white plaques approximately 1 mm. in diameter.

ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA BLADDER TRAUMA EUTHANASIA. This 9-year-old female gazelle presented for routine ovariohysterectomy which was uncomplicated. When the animal recovered from anesthesia it showed signs of severe colic with repeated straining. An exploratory laparotomy was performed and the animal aspirated ruminal contents while being intubated. Exploration showed no problems related to the surgery. The animal became anuric despite high volume intravenous fluids and diuretics failed to respond to therapy and was euthanized for humane and diagnostic purposes. Necropsy showed aspirated ruminal material throughout all pulmonary fields. The kidneys had pale streaking over the cortices and some nodules were in the spleen. The mucosa of the urinary bladder was reddened. Cecal contents were inspissated and partially adhered to the mucosa.

MULTICENTRIC ABSCESSES DYSTROPHIC MINERALIZATION AND DEGENERATIVE CARDIAC DISEASE. This 13.5-year-old tree kangaroo had a history of suspected cardiac disease with enteroliths a calcified lesion or abscess in the cervical region and multiple subcutaneous inguinal granulomas. A previous biopsy of a mass from the inguinal region identified necrotic fat (G12-0675). The animal had been maintained for cardiac disease for 1.5 years but then died. Necropsy revealed a 3 cm. encapsulated mass in the right cervical area numerous 1-3 mm. firm white masses in the inguinal area 200 ml. of serous fluid in the thoracic cavity dark pink to congested lungs that floated in formalin. The apex of the heart was firm and rubbery. On cut surface the apex of the left ventricle contained a 2-3 cm. caseous friable tan/brown mass that was adhered to and infiltrating the ventricular free wall and interventricular septum. In the peritoneal cavity there were 50 ml. of serous fluid and 2-3 cm. gastroliths were present in the stomach. Several 1-2 mm. firm white nodules were in the testes.

BACTERIAL DERMATITIS CLOACITIS MYONECROSIS. This 9-year-old male rattlesnake was under treatment for tail lesions and was found dead. At necropsy dermatitis with necrosis was noted at the base of the rattle.

PULMONARY SHOCK PROBABLE ASPHYXIATION (TUNNEL ENTRAPMENT) HEPATOCELLULAR NODULAR HYPERPLASIA. This 2.5-year-old male prairie dog was found dead in a tunnel and was new to the enclosure. Necropsy revealed good body condition sand in the front of the mouth and nares laxity in the mandibular symphysis exposure of the root of the left lower incisor dark lungs and two 3 mm. in diameter pale masses in two hepatic lobes.

TRAUMA (ENTRAPMENT) PULMONARY SHOCK. This 4-month-old male lemur was found dead by a keeper in the enclosure moat with its maxilla stuck in a feeder. Examination revealed shivering and hypothermia. Supportive care was administered but the patient became obtunded and died during attempts to intubate. Resuscitation attempts were unsuccessful. Necropsy revealed frothy serosanguineous discharge in the oral cavity and both nostrils a large amount of gas trapped in the pleural space and marked pulmonary consolidation. Negative pressure was not observed in the thorax when the diaphragm was punctured. No air leakage was noted when the lungs were insufflated at necropsy. Three of the five pulmonary lobes sank in formalin a small amount of serous pericardial fluid was in the pericardial sac and a contusion was in the left atrial free wall. A moderate amount of gas was in the retroperitoneal space.

RETINAL DEGENERATION EUTHANASIA. This 7-year-old female lion presented 13 days prior to death with an acute onset of severe ataxia. She was alert and responsive with good appetite. She had a 4-6 month history of progressive visual deficits. At presentation for ataxia she could not follow close movement could not see her food when offered could see large dark objects moving at a distance. She could hear and smell. Initial blood work and radiographs were within normal limits. A threefold lower titer to canine distemper was detected compared to values obtained at the previous annual exam. The cat has negative titers to Toxoplasma FeLV and FIP. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was within normal limits and cerebrospinal fluid titers were negative to Toxoplasma and canine distemper. The animal did not respond to steroid administration. An MRI was performed three days prior to death and the only lesion noted was some minimal enhancement of the left optic nerve. The cat was unable to move from right lateral recumbency after the MRI even with glucocorticoid and diuretic therapy. Euthanasia was elected due to the poor prognosis. This animal had a cub die of presumed canine distemper two years ago. Recently a snow leopard at the Columbia Park Zoo in West Lafayette Indiana had a similar history. Necropsy revealed pressure sores on the right side of the body. Subcutaneous edema was generalized on the right side of the body. All internal organs were normal. No significant findings were in the brain. Bilateral symmetrical areas on the cerebellum resembled a bruise but symmetry suggests normal structure.

METASTATIC MINERALIZATION RENAL GOUT. This 4-year-old female lorikeet was found dead in exhibit. At necropsy there were small white fuzzy masses in the air sacs and on the organs. The kidneys were discolored and mottled.

PERITONEAL SPINDLE CELL SARCOMA PULMONARY EDEMA AND CONGESTION SHOCK. This 5-year/1-month-old neutered male domestic goat died suddenly in the early afternoon. It had been doing fine and had eaten that morning. At necropsy the lungs were mottled and had interstitial congestion. The right cranial lung lobe was firm and had a cobblestone appearance. The bronchi appeared to be thicker than those in the other normal lung lobes. The heart had white myocardial streaks in both ventricles. There was a 2.5 cm. long leather-like texture foreign body within the rumen. There were adhesions and fibrinous tags to the body wall diaphragm and liver. There was a large 15 x 11 x 2.5 cm. mass present within the abdomen. It had strong adhesions to the body wall and was connected to the ventral sac of the rumen. The mass was yellow/white very friable and full of yellow gel-like material. The wall was thick and contained inspissated material. The peritoneal cavity contained approximately 20 ml. of clear yellow fluid.

EUTHANASIA BACTERIAL GRANULOMAS MYOCARDIAL FIBROSIS PANCREATIC DEGENERATION. This greater than 18-year-old male rattlesnake was humanely euthanized. It had a chronic history of weight loss anorexia and a recent tail abscess that responded partially to treatment. The animal was receiving support treatment including fluids and force feeding with no response. It was becoming progressively weak and encountering difficulties in maneuvering in its exhibit. At necropsy it was thin and had poor scale quality. The caudal one-third of the coelom contained straw colored fluid distending the retrocoelomic space. The large vessels of the heart and hepatic and mesenteric vessels were distended and tortuous. There were multiple nodular black areas along the right lateral heart under the pericardium that extended cranially along the large vessels. The nodules were 0.5 x 0.5 cm. soft and oozed dark blood on cut surface. The heart wall appeared very flabby. There was a 2 x 1.5 cm. tan mass on the surface of the distal colon. On section the mass was homogeneous and was associated with narrowing of the intestine. The kidneys appeared firm on cut surface.
ACUTE YOLK COELOMITIS. This 1-year-old female teal was found dead. Its only medical history is an injured leg approximately one year ago. Necropsy revealed advanced autolysis and possible coelomitis.

TRAUMA. This 5-year-old female ruddy duck was inadvertently netted two weeks earlier and was caught in the net for an extended period of time developing shock. Supportive care was administered the bird responded and was returned to exhibit. The day before death the keepers had drained the pool in the exhibit and the duck was found dead the following morning. Necropsy revealed bilaterally severely congested lungs good body condition and minimal ingesta in the gastrointestinal tract.

EUTHANASIA ARTHRITIS (CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS) CHRONIC ENTERITIS. This 18-year-old female sheep had a history of chronic illness blindness and arthritis. The animal was humanely euthanized. At necropsy the heart was thin and dark tan.

CUTANEOUS ROUND CELL NEOPLASM OOPHORITIS. This 12-year-old female Honduran milk snake had multiple dermal masses that became disseminated over a several week period. Previous biopsy (G16-2667) was suggestive of a round cell tumor. It is not stated if this animal died spontaneously or was euthanized. The left gonad was firm and the right gonad was indistinct. Multiple spherical swellings were within the coelomic cavity.

CHRONIC NEPHRITIS MYOCARDIAL FIBROSIS ENTERITIS ORGANIZING HEMATOMA (LIVER). This 11-year-old female capybara was found in acute respiratory distress. The animal died prior to treatment. At necropsy a light tan soft mass was present in the cervical region containing caseous material.  A similar mass was present on the right lateral neck. Tricuspid valve leaflets were thickened irregular and white. Dark red lobulated masses were present in the mesentery and adjacent to the liver.

INANITION BILIARY CYST BACTERIAL SPLENITIS RETAINED SPECTACLE. This 11-year-old female copperhead had a recent history of dysecdysis. The animal was found dead. At necropsy the adrenal was irregular and enlarged. White nodules were present in the liver.

INANITION RENAL ADENOMA PULMONARY SHOCK URATE STASIS. This 10-year-old male duck was caught for a wing trim and examination. The animal was thin at that time. The following day the animal was found weak and depressed and died before treatment could be initiated. At necropsy the bird was emaciated with no adipose stores. Focal dark red patches were present in the lung. The liver contained several 2-3 mm. white plaques on the capsule.

EUTHANASIA ARTHRITIS (CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS) ADENOCARCINOMA (UTERUS MESENTERY) HEPATIC ADENOMA HEPATIC HEMOSIDEROSIS EXTRAMEDULLARY HEMATOPOIESIS CHRONIC NEPHRITIS. This 17-year-old female potbellied pig was euthanized due to declining quality of life and severe arthritis. At necropsy overgrowth of the claws of the fourth limbs was noted. Firm irregular masses were present in the liver. Cyst-like lesions containing clear fluid were associated with the bile duct. Irregular white masses were also present in the spleen mesenteric root and uterus.

ESOPHAGEAL ADENOCARCINOMA INTERRENAL CELL ADENOMA EUTHANASIA. This 41-year-old male ground boa had been doing poorly for several months. Supportive therapy was attempted with no improvement and euthanasia was performed for humane and diagnostic purposes. Necropsy revealed thin body condition no external lesions minimal fat stores clotted blood in the pericardial sac (euthanasia) empty alimentary tract enlarged abnormal-appearing testicle white streaking in the kidneys and no other abnormalities. The right testicle was not identified.

METASTATIC MINERALIZATION. This 13-year-old female chuckwalla has a history of blepharitis involving the right eyelid was receiving supportive care and also had chronic weight loss. The animal was found dead in the morning. Necropsy revealed areas of hepatic pallor mild fat atrophy enlarged kidneys containing multiple punctate white foci and highly vascular and reddened left ovary and right ovary.

AMYLOIDOSIS EMACIATION STRESS. This 13-year-old male white-faced whistling duck was behaving irregularly and found dead. There were heavy thunderstorms in the morning. At necropsy the liver was firm and shrunken.

DISSEMINATED INFECTIOUS DISEASE PROCESS INTESTINAL NEMATODIASIS OVARIAN ADENOCARCINOMA. This 2.5-year-old female parrot was found dead in the morning with no prior signs of illness. Necropsy revealed bilateral periorbital edema and moderate subcutaneous hemorrhage caudal medial to the left eye. Body condition was thin. Female gonad was identified. The brain appeared edematous. Multiple petechiae were noted across the surface of the cranium.

EUTHANASIA RENAL AMYLOIDOSIS CHRONIC NEPHRITIS TRANSITIONAL CELL CARCINOMA (MESENTERY SPLEEN) BILIARY CYST. This 7-year-old ferret presented with polyuria anorexia and weight loss. The animal was humanely euthanized due to chronic renal failure. At necropsy the animal was thin and dehydrated. A small soft tissue mass was present near the abdominal aorta and kidney. Kidneys were irregular and pale.

BOTRYOMYCOSIS EPICARDIAL ADHESIONS CARDIAC INSUFFICIENCY EUTHANASIA. This 6-year-old male squirrel monkey had been the lowest ranking monkey in the troupe. It had been examined for multiple wounds associated with conspecific aggression. The animal developed weakness lethargy and anemia with respiratory distress presumably due to heart failure. Euthanasia was performed for humane and diagnostic purposes. Necropsy revealed numerous wounds and hair loss along the back and legs distended abdomen with palpable fluid wave alopecic skin on the tail numerous areas of ulceration and crust formation along the dorsum 7 ml. of pink tinged effusion in the thoracic cavity severe diffuse right-sided pulmonary edema and consolidation on the ventral aspects of the left lung 4 ml. of yellow pericardial effusion thickened pericardial sac with white plaques 25 ml. of mildly sanguineous ascites diffusely rounded and congested liver numerous prominent lymph nodes in the mandibular cervical and colonic regions mottled white/pink/red kidneys with reduced corticomedullary distinction and numerous intramuscular encapsulated abscesses.

BACTERIAL/FOREIGN BODY COELOMITIS TRAUMA. This 7-year-old female white bellied stork was found in moribund condition and recumbent in the river exhibit with multiple wounds. A second stork was found dead at the same time also with wounds. Necropsy revealed good nutritional status and several puncture wounds in the pectoral muscles and lateral thighs. The lungs were diffusely and bilaterally hemorrhagic. Tan turbid granular fluid was free in the caudal coelomic cavity and in the same area was a fibrinous possibly purulent covering of the serosal surface of most of the intestinal tract proventriculus and ventriculus caudal liver ovary kidneys air sacs and spleen. A dark necrotic area was on the serosal surface of the ventriculus but no perforation was noted.

INANITION. This 4-year-old leiothrix had a history of egg binding. The bird was found dead. At necropsy the oviduct was enlarged and friable. Adhesions were present between the liver and intestinal tract.

ACUTE VASCULAR SHOCK POSSIBLE THORACIC TRAUMA. This 8-year-old male colobus was found dead with no prior signs of illness. Necropsy revealed advanced postmortem autolysis. The body was in excellent nutritional status. A small amount of foamy hemorrhagic fluid was in the subcutaneous space on the lateral aspect of the abdomen. All organs were in an advanced state of postmortem autolysis. The lungs were congested with blood but floated in formalin. The heart was grossly enlarged with the right atrium and vessels leading into the right atrium severely distended with blood clots. A small amount of red/brown fluid was in the pericardial sac. Multiple petechiae to ecchymotic hemorrhages were on the surface of the heart. Lighter areas of discoloration are detected throughout the musculature of the heart. Approximately 200 ml. of red/brown fluid was in the abdominal cavity. A small portion of the capsule of the spleen is torn off. The liver has a fibrous texture on cut surface. Food is in the digested tract.

DIC RHABDOMYOLYSIS LUMPY JAW PULMONARY BACTERIAL ABSCESSES LYMPH NODE GRANULOMA. This 22-year-old male giraffe was found dead in the morning. It was scheduled for an immobilization that day. The animal had been having bilateral forelimb hoof issues since 2007 and had become progressively stiffer in the forelimbs since that time. The immobilization procedure was for a hoof trim. There is also a past history of a mass removal on the face. Necropsy revealed swelling of the fetlock and pastern joints of the forelimbs overgrowth of the hoof walls of these legs with the medial and lateral claws deviating from midline a 5 cm. mass in the maxillary region of the right side of the head cranial to the first premolar that on cut surface was firm with mild amounts of purulent material expressed with digital pressure. Adipose stores in the subcutaneous and pericardial regions had serous atrophy. Superficial musculature of the left hind limb was pale. Ruminal fluid was present in the tracheal lumen. Two well encapsulated 5 cm. masses were in the left caudal pulmonary lobe. One parabronchial lymph node was enlarged. A small amount of yellow nonviscous fluid was present in the pericardial sac. The gallbladder was pale but not thickened.
EUTHANASIA HEMOSIDEROSIS HEPATITIS COLITIS. This greater than 32-year-old female skink presented with neurologic signs and was humanely euthanized. At necropsy the skink was in poor body condition.
adult. Weight: 2500.0 g.  Gall stone; kidney haemorrhage; kidney cyst.

COELOMITIS BACTERIAL COELOMITIS METASTATIC ADENOCARCINOMA. This 5-year-old female chicken has a history of weight loss and lethargy. Treatment was initiated; however the animal later died. Inspissated follicles were embedded within the mass. A small white nodule was present in the liver and spleen.

EUTHANASIA CHRONIC NEPHRITIS MYOCARDIAL FIBROSIS PULMONARY EDEMA. This 12-year-old female rabbit was euthanized. At necropsy the heart was rounded and enlarged. Kidneys were small and irregular. Hemorrhage was noted adjacent to the lumbar vertebrae and spinal cord.

RENAL GOUT. This 1.5-year-old captive bred female lory was found dead on floor. It was wet but not near water dish. At necropsy it had excessive fat stores. There were no signs of trauma. The air sacs were clear. The spleen was slightly enlarged. The crop had no food and a small black spot. There was no feed material in the proventriculus or gizzard.

DEGENERATIVE CARDIAC AND RENAL DISEASE LARYNGEAL MASS GRANULOSA CELL TUMOR EUTHANASIA. This 25-year-old female squirrel monkey had a history of arteriosclerosis a laryngeal mass and progressive respiratory distress. Euthanasia was performed for humane and diagnostic purposes. Necropsy revealed a pink semifirm irregular slightly pedunculated mass to 0.5 cm. in greatest dimension that occluded approximately of the larynx. The ascending aorta was roughened on its intimal surface. Some crepitation was noted in this region of the vessel and at the aortic bifurcation. The kidneys were slightly pale.
INANITION. This 11-year-old female toad has a several month history of inactivity. The animal was found dead. No significant gross lesions were noted at necropsy.

YOLK COELOMITIS CHRONIC OOPHORITIS INANITION. This 20-year-old female tortoise was found dead. At necropsy the GI tract was distended with gas. Urate concretions were present in the bladder. Coelomic fat depots were absent. Lungs contained frothy fluid.

EUTHANASIA ESOPHAGEAL CANDIDIASIS INANITION HEPATOCELLULAR HEMOSIDEROSIS. This 7-year-old male bat was under treatment for weight loss and weakness. The animal was found down and was euthanized due to poor prognosis. At necropsy large holes were noted in the wing membranes. The GI tract was devoid of ingesta and was gas filled.

BACTERIAL MENINGITIS PNEUMONIA SHOCK. This 13-year-old male wallaroo presented with ataxia and lethargy. Treatment was initiated; however there was no improvement and the animal was humanely euthanized.

METASTATIC MINERALIZATION. This 16-year-old male Siberian tiger has a history of arthritis and chronic regurgitation. The animal had a one week history of increased respiratory rate and was found dead. Necropsy revealed red raised lesions distributed throughout the surface of the urinary bladder dark red lungs thyroid cysts and a raised nodule on the luminal surface of the stomach near the pylorus.

CIRRHOSIS HERNIATED HEPATIC LOBE EUTHANASIA. This 8-year-old female cottontop tamarin has a history of biliary cirrhosis and bacterial cholangiohepatitis associated with herniation of a hepatic lobe (G13-1039). Exploratory surgery was performed and a large mass effect was noted in one lobe of the liver. Euthanasia was performed for humane and diagnostic purposes. Necropsy revealed thin body condition multiple cysts present in the left lateral and quadrate lobes of the liver adhesions of the diaphragm to the diaphragmatic surface of the liver apparent right medial hepatic lobe involvement in the previously described hernia petechiae on the serosal surface of the left kidney a 3 mm. depression in the cortex of the right kidney that contained inspissated duct material distended colon and no other abnormalities.

PULMONARY EDEMA INTERSTITIAL PNEUMONIA. This 13-year-old male merganser presented with ataxia weakness and weight loss. At necropsy the bird was thin. The liver was enlarged and pale. The spleen was markedly enlarged.

INTERSTITIAL PNEUMONIA HEPATITIS SPLENITIS. This 11-year-old female penguin was dehydrated and inappetent. The animal was restrained for examination but collapsed and died shortly after the exam was finished. Resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful. At necropsy lungs were thickened white and sank in formalin. Heart had white foci.

SEPTIC PERITONITIS GUT CONTENTS IN ABDOMEN EUTHANASIA. This 3.5-year-old female wallaby had surgery to remove an abscess from the colonic mesentery but subsequently presented with septic abdomen and colonic rupture. Euthanasia was performed for humane and diagnostic purposes. Necropsy revealed fair body condition gut contents in the abdominal cavity pale gray tissue at the resection site and some purple/black mucosal lesions near the distal pylorus. No other gross abnormalities were noted. Histologic examination of the colonic abscess revealed granulomatous lymphadenitis in which mycobacteria were identified.

All of the live birds were in production with an average clutch size of 5 ova. The average abdominal fat pad thickness was 2 mm including two birds with 1 mm fat pads. There were 1 to 3 pieces of large particle limestone within the ventriculus (gizzard) with the majority of the birds having none. Two of the live birds had collapsed ribs. One had moderate and 2 had mild beading of the ribs. Two birds had a recent keel fracture of the distal free end of the keel bone. One bird had a moderate and 2 birds had mild T-2 mycotoxin oral lesions. All but 2 of the dead birds were in production. Body fat was adequate. None of the dead birds had large particle limestone within the ventriculus (gizzard). Seven of the dead birds had collapsed rib cages. Four birds had a recent keel fracture of the distal free end of the keel bone. Four birds had S-shaped keel bones. One bird died from hypocalcemia. Two birds had egg yolk peritonitis. One bird had ovarian hemorrhage. One bird had ovarian adenocarcinoma (tumor). One bird had fatty liver syndrome. One bird had a fractured leg with associated hemorrhage. One bird had gout. Two birds had mild T-2 mycotoxin oral lesions Osteomalacia Egg yolk peritonitis Ovarian adenocarcinoma Hemorrhage; ovary Fatty liver syndrome Fracture; femur Visceral gout Hypocalcemia Comment: The cause of death in this flock of chickens is due to multiple causes based upon the gross lesions. The contribution of osteomalacia to those causes could not be speculated upon. The causes of death not related to lack of calcium are ovarian adenocarcinoma; hemorrhage of the ovary; fatty liver syndrome and gout. Additional testing is being performed and a final report will be generated when that testing is completed. If you have any questions or concerns; feel free to contact me at 517-353-3701.

EUTHANASIA SPONDYLOSIS INANITION. This 17-year-old male rattlesnake had a one year history of spinal fusion. The animal was humanely euthanized due to declining quality of life. At necropsy the animal was thin. The vertebrae along two-thirds of the length of the spine were fused.

SARCOCYSTOSIS. This greater than 5-year-old female lorikeet was found on the ground with respiratory distress received supportive care but was found dead in the morning. Necropsy revealed lean body condition edema in the lungs the lungs sank in formalin multiple tan foci in the parenchyma of the liver a small amount of nectar in the crop a small amount of gritty material in the ventriculus two tan-colored masses on the serosal surface of the spleen and no other abnormalities.

INTESTINAL NEMATODIASIS INANITION DERMATITIS. This 3-year-old toad was found dead. The animal recently had an abrasion on the forearm and was treated with antibiotics. At necropsy the frog was thin with scant fat stores. A smooth white erosion was present over the left scapula and medial aspect of the right femur. The gall bladder was distended with thick yellow fluid.

EUTHANASIA MYOPATHY GRANULOMATOUS LYMPHADENITIS SUSPECT TRAUMA. This female greater than 8-year-old peccary was humanely euthanized due to nonimproving rear limb paresis and paralysis. This peccary was reported as mildly off the week prior to death; however it essentially visually returned to normal within 36 hours. About 48 hours prior to presentation for paresis the keepers reported that the peccary never returned to normal attitude. It presented for inability to stand on the rear limbs on 1/22. No lesions were detected on radiographs of the spine pelvis limbs and ribs. At necropsy there was heavy muscled and carried moderate fat reserves subcutaneously. No external trauma could be identified. The distal trachea and cervical tissues were intensely hemorrhagic and the heart contained friable blood clots (euthanasia artifact). The dentition was heavily stained with mild accumulations of dental tartar at the gingival borders of the buccal surfaces of the molars. Ingesta and digesta were present in the stomach and intestines respectively. The mucosa of the intestine appeared reddened in multiple sites. The ovaries were active with the left containing a substantial corpus luteum. The uterine horns had occasional pockets along the endometrium that on cut section released a creamy yellow/white fluid. The uterine lumen was empty of fluid or debris. The ventral epaxial musculature had mildly ecchymotic areas along the caudal thoracic and thoracolumbar spinal column. Dissection through the dorsal epaxial musculature ventrally to the vertebrae did not reveal any additional hemorrhage nor were any fractures identified. The thoracolumbar spinal cord itself was substantially softer than the sections cranial and caudal to it. The space surrounding the thoracolumbar spinal cord was also filled with darkly congested blood that was not present cranially and caudally. The epaxial muscle bellies had substantial areas of paleness throughout them. This was more severe in the rear limbs throughout the thigh and gluteal muscles bilaterally. Sections of heart lung liver kidney spleen and stomach contents were frozen for future use if needed.

RHABDOMYOLYSIS SHOCK POSSIBLE HYPERTHERMIA. This 13-year-old male common squirrel monkey presented with lateral recumbency and was poorly responsive and had high fever. Necropsy revealed bright pink lungs that bled substantially on cut surface. The stomach was distended with gas and fluid and was extremely thin walled and nearly transparent. No rugae were seen in the mucosa. Mild light red to purple speckling was noted in the parenchyma of the liver the intestine was distended with gas a small amount of fluid and was extremely thin walled a small amount of bruising was in the scrotum and the epididymis of the left testicle was bruised. Shortly before death the monkey passed a white opaque firmly gelatinous material from the penis and a small amount of this material was also seen in the urinary bladder.

DEGENERATIVE JOINT DISEASE ARTERIOSCLEROSIS EUTHANASIA. This 16-year-old male bat was euthanized for humane and diagnostic purposes and had a history of wing mutilation and osteoarthritis. CLOSTRIDIAL ENTERITIS HEPATITIS BACTERMIA. This 10-month-old lory was treated with antibiotics and antiprotozoals approximately three months prior to death. The animal was found dead. At necropsy the duodenum contained an area of hemorrhage. The cloaca was also hemorrhagic.

EUTHANASIA THYROID CARCINOMA CHRONIC PROGRESSIVE NEPHROPATHY HEART FAILURE. This male 26-month-old rat was humanely euthanized. It had a history of weight loss (150 gm. since April). BACTERIAL ENTERITIS SPLENITIS SEPTICEMIA. This 8-year-old toad had a history of repeated bloating episodes. Treatment was initiated; however the animal later died. At necropsy the superficial skin was sloughing. Serosanguineous fluid was present in the coelomic cavity and subcutis.

PROLIFERATIVE ENTERITIS RENAL GOUT METASTATIC MINERALIZATION FLAGELLATE ENTERITIS EUTHANASIA. This 16-year-old male monitor was euthanized for humane and diagnostic purposes. ENTERITIS SHOCK. This 3-year-old male lory was found dead. At gross necropsy internal organs had diffuse congestion.
PREDATION (CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS) ENTERITIS. This 40-year-old female flamingo was attacked by a fox. At necropsy the cervical vertebrae and trachea were transected.

BACTERIAL ENTERITIS WITH SEPSIS. This 16-year-old female mandrill tested positive for simian foamy virus and has a history of papillomas on the face. NUTRITIONAL BONE DISEASE EUTHANASIA. This 11-month-old smoky jungle frog of undetermined gender was euthanized. MYCOTIC DERMATITIS HEPATIC AMYLOIDOSIS GLOMERULAR AMYLOIDOSIS RENAL GOUT INANITION. This 13-year-old male swan was under treatment for weight loss and blistering of the skin on the feet and beak. PANCREATIC FIBROSIS DIABETES MELLITUS. This 7-year-old female rock hyrax has a history of enlarged uterus that was removed surgically in fall 1999. The animal was from a group of hyrax in which diabetes mellitus associated with islet fibrosis has been diagnosed histologically. Exploratory surgery and pancreatic biopsy revealed severe islet fibrosis warranting a poor prognosis. The animal was euthanized for humane reasons. Blood was drawn for CBC serum chemistry and serum bank and the animal was euthanized for necropsy. The pancreas was photographed in situ and on cut surface. Necropsy revealed good body condition with minor fat reserves. Slight wide streaking was in the muscle of the ventricular epicardium. The pancreas was enlarged and firm (1.5 x 1 x 0.5 cm.) and seemed fibrotic on cut surface. The omentum contained several small to medium sized firm yellow nodules resembling necrotic fat. At necropsy the heart was pale. There were large fat bodies in the coelom. There was 3 cm. long firm caseated material located in the left hemipenes region that was cultured.

GASTRIC ULCER SEPSIS RENAL TUBULAR NECROSIS. This 9-year-old female chinchilla was found moribund in an education holding exhibit and had lost 18% of its weight over a three month interval. HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMAS CHRONIC HEPATOPATHY EXERTIONAL MYOPATHY. This 12-year-old female Thomson’s gazelle had been treated for severe hypothermia and suspected capture myopathy with associated azotemia and was found dead the following morning. Necropsy revealed obesity dark and heavy lungs a white scar on the surface of the lung a large amount of cavitary fat firm cavitary fat approximately 100 ml. of sanguineous fluid in the peritoneal cavity dark discoloration of the ruminal papillae rounded hepatic margins possible ruptured gallbladder and a 7 cm. expansile mass in the hepatic parenchyma with associated yellow discoloration and extensive vasculature. Two other hepatic masses were also noted. The intestine was dark purple. Intraluminal masses were in the cervix uterine body and uterine horns. Dark red fluid was in the urinary bladder.

This aged male vasectomized chimpanzee had been the subject of severe conspecific aggression two days previous to death (8 Jan 2016) with mulitple bite wounds that were treated with flushing; local debridement; and antibiotic therapy. He at first improved; then on the second day; became increasingly compromised. He had a cardiac arrest shortly after immobilization for further diagnostics (10 Jan 2016). Necropsy was performed on 12 January 2016 at 1300 hrs. Examined is an aged male chimpanzee with an inner right thigh tattoo 649; weighing 65.5 kg; with a body condition score of approximately 4/9. He was well hydrated and there was moderate autolysis. There were numerous severe wounds: An irregular laceration of the upper left lip measuring approximately 10 x 4 x 0.5 cm with a significant missing fragment; a 2 cm long laceration over the right eye; a 2.5 cm laceration over the right cranial ear cartilage; a 2 cm deep laceration over the left elbow; and many lacerations; often extending to the bone on the digits of the hands and feet. The distal 2 phalanges of the 5th phalanx of the left foot was missing. An irregular 6 cm long laceration of the scrotum. A 5 x 5 cm wide region of skin was missing and the deeper tissues soft and gray/green in an arc over the dorsum of the anus and extending partially into the anal canal. All wounds were soft and weeping variable amounts of viscous exudate. Both upper canine teeth were absent as well as lateral incisors There was minimal subcutaneous; internal; pericardial; and perirenal fat. Within the abdominal cavity; the mesentery was tacky; moderately opaque; and adhered to the body wall; the serosa of most of the intestines; the spleen; and the urinary bladder. In the thorax; the lungs had extensive areas of dark red discoloration (hemorrhage) around the hilus on the dorsum of the heart (approximately 5 x 3 cm on the right and 10 x 2 cm on the left and the right immediately adjacent to the hilus). The epicardium of the heart was moderately streaked with pale areas especially over the ventricles; and in some areas this extended into the myocardium. Especially of note was a region of pallor in the free wall of the left ventricle extending transmurally. The liver was firm with rounded edges and dark red to brown. It weighed 1490.3 g (2.3% body weight). The urinary bladder was severely distended with urine; measuring 19 x 14 x 9 cm (holding over 2 L of clear urine). Skin; rectum; lip; scrotum: Severe multifocal traumatic lacerations with secondary necrosis Digits: Severe lacerations and traumatic amputation Heart: Moderate myocardial fibrosis (presumptive; pending histopathology) Urinary bladder: Distention and possible neurogenic distention Abdominal cavity: Chronic mild peritonitis with adhesions Lungs: Moderate hilar hemorrhage (likely due to CPR) Prostate: Mild prostatic hyperplasia Testicle (left): Moderate atrophy Epdididymi: Bilateral granulomatous epididymitis (sperm granulomas - secondary to vasectomy) Stifle; hip (bilaterally): Moderate degenerative arthropathy Vertebra (L1; L2): Focal nodular osseous proliferation Comment: At this point; a clear cause of death is not evident. The wounds did not appear to cause peritonitis (the changes in the abdomen are too chronic and low-grade); nor did the chimp appear septic at the time of death. The appearance of fibrosis in the heart is of concern; as heart disease is common in aged male chimps. The cause for the retention of urine in the bladder is not clear - neurogenic causes are most likely and so the spinal cord has been removed to the point of the cauda equina for microscopic inspection. The reproductive and musculoskeletal changes are expected in an animal of this age; and the lung lesions were likely secondary to CPR. Additional data and photographs are on file with the recorded weights of organs and the Great Ape Heart Project protocol data on the heart. These will be held on file at the DCPAH and sent to the zoo and the SSP pathologist for chimps. Histopathology is pending and a final report will give these results. Multiple frozen tissues are on file as well and will not be discarded without the zoo's notice so that they may be retrieved if desired Examined are sections of eye (block 1); left and right trigeminal; pituitary gland (2); left and right testicle; epididymi (3-6); heart apex (7); apex; left outflow tract (7); left ventricle (9-10); right ventricle (11); aorta (arch); left ventricle (12); hemorrhoid (13); prostatic urethra (14); liver (15); skin (16); adrenal glands (17); tongue; intestine (18); intestines; salivary gland (19-20); kidney (21); kidney; spleen (22); trachea; airsac (23); bone marrow (24); thyroid gland (25); stomach; pancreas (26-27); urethra; trigone; seminal vesicle (28); prostate; seminal vesicle (29); lung (30-31); brain (32-36); spinal cord (caudal cord L3-S) (37); spinal cord (cranial T; C); brachial plexus (39); and bone (vertebral mass)(40). In almost all areas of the heart; there are multifocal bands of mature fibrosis separating bundles of cardiac myocytes and sometimes isolating individual fibers. In many areas; the myocytes are shrunken; vacuolated; and sometimes pale staining. There is marked anisokaryosis and pleomorphism among nuclei; and in some muscle fibers; there are aggregated bundles of nuclei. In the aorta; there is a single focus of mineralization which disrupts the contour of the intima and projects into the lumen. In the lung; there is some peripheral consolidation and collapse. Throughout the lung; there are marked congestion and frequent individal and small aggregates of hemosiderin laden alveolar macrophages. In one bronchiole; there is abundant mucus and many large vacuolated macrophages. In the liver; there is marked congestion and degeneration of central hepatocytes; as well as abundant agggregates of hemosiderin within Kupffer cells concentrated in the centrilobular areas. In some areas; there is frank necrosis and fibrin plaques lining sinusoids. In the adrenal gland; there are several nodular foci of cortical cell hyperplasia within and beyond the capsule. In the cortex; the fasciulata and reticularis cells have abundant lipofuscin within Heart: Severe interstitial fibrosis and myocardial degeneration Lung: Moderate atelectasis and alveolar histiocytosis with hemosiderin Liver: Moderate diffuse centrilobular degeneration; mild multifocal necrosis; and moderate hemosiderosis Kidney; spleen; intestines: Severe congestion Testicles: Mild degeneration with epididymal dilation Tongue: Superficial bacterial colonization and superficial hemorrhage Adrenal gland: Multifocal nodular hyperplasia; moderate cortical lipofusinosis Aorta: Mild focal intimal mineralization Comment: The cause of death in this chimp was most likely cardiac failure as a result of the severe myocardial fibrosis and degeneration compounded by the stress of the traumatic injuries and anesthesia. Cardiac fibrosis is a very common finding in aged chimpanzees (particularly males); though a specific cause has not been identified. These changes were clearly long-standing with evidence in the lung of left-sided heart failure and more recent evidence of right-sided heart failure in the liver and other abdominal organs. The other changes are likely age related and/or sequela from the trauma and heart disease. Review of the brain tissues and the spinal cord are pending. An explanation for the urinary bladder distension and inability to empty at the time of necropsy is not present in the tissue examined. An addendum report will address any additional findings and should be completed in the next few days. The information requested by the Great Ape Heart Project will be collated and provided to the SSP pathologist; Dr. Karen Terio Additional diagnoses: Spinal cord: Mild arterial hyaline degeneration Vertebral body (L1-2): Osteochondroma Comment: The arterial changes in the spinal cord are likely incidental and age-related. Osteochondromas are benign developmental abnormalites that arise along growth plates in a variety of locations and have been reported in many species. Usually they are reported when they are intraspinal and cause compression of the spinal cord. In this case; the tumor was extraspinal and unlikely to have caused any clinical signs. This completes testing on this case. Frozen archived tissues will be held in the Agnew research laboratory unless the zoo would prefer to hold these in their facility

\_ apocrine; mild granulomatous inflammation - MNG cells inbetween scar tiss Heart: Multifocal myocardial necrosis with mild myocardial fibrosis and regeneration Lung: Marked chronic pulmonary edema with alveolar histiocytosis Kidney: Marked multifocal chronic renal infarction and interstitial nephritis; generalized membranous glomerulopathy; and multifocal tubular necrosis Liver: Mild multifocal centrolobular hepatic necrosis Subcutis: Please see comment Comment The pattern of histologic findings supported heart disease with severe pulmonary edema (heart failure) as the likely cause of death in this patient. Hypoxic damage was also evidenced in the kidney (tubular necrosis) and liver (centrolobular necrosis). No specific etiology for the underlying heart disease was apparent. Underlying chronic kidney disease also likely affected the overall health of this animal and may have been complicated by concurrent dehydration. The subcutaneous proliferative epithelial lesion was surrounded by fibroplasia; consistent with scarring from previous surgery. Although cellular deterioration interfered with classification of the lesion; the findings were most suggestive of a glandular neoplasm of apocrine gland origin. TTF-1 immunolabeling was performed and did not support a bronchogenic epithelial origin. Apocrine gland neoplasms may arise from adnexa of the haired skin or mammary glands; and according to a retrospective study in African hedgehogs; mammary gland adenocarcinomas are the most common tumor of the integumentary system; occurring along the ventral thorax as well as abdomen. In this case; cellular features did not clearly indicate malignancy; therefore an adenoma or a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma were considered. It was not apparent that this proliferative lesion contributed directly to the animal's death. Reference: Raymond JT and Garner MM. Left kidney: Primary renal neoplasia Right kidney: Multifocal renal nodules; consistent with neoplasia COMMENTS The most common primary renal neoplasms in animals include carcinoma of renal tubular epithelial origin; nephroblastoma; and transitional cell carcinoma. Histopathology is underway to further characterize the neoplasm. The nodules in the right kidney may represent metastatic spread of the primary tumor or may represent independently arising multicentric disease. No gross evidence of metastasis was found in other organs. Results of histopathology will be provided in a final report. Jana M. Ritter; DVM See preliminary report. Kidney: Primary renal sarcoma; Chronic moderate interstitial nephritis with edema; fibrosis; and severe tubular ectasia Intestine: Acute severe segmental suppurative enteritis with submucosal hemorrhage and edema Heart: Moderate multifocal necrotizing myocarditis Pancreas: Locally extensive chronic active fibrosing peripancreatic steatitis Lymph node: Chronic lymphadenitis with moderate subcapsular histiocytosis Stomach: Mild multifocal pustular gastritis Primary renal sarcoma (See comments) COMMENTS Primary renal sarcomas are rare in animals and likely arise from neoplastic transformation of interstitial stromal cells. The findings of neoplasia in both kidneys; but not in other organs; is suggestive of spread from one kidney to the other by implantation. Findings in the small intestine are suggestive of acute penetrating trauma. While renal neoplasia is the most apparent cause for the clinical signs observed prior to euthanasia; acute enteritis may have exacerbated those signs. Changes described in the heart are probably age-related. Peripancreatic findings are indicate chronic active inflammation of undetermined origin. Jana M. Ritter; DVM

PHAEOHYPHOMYCOSIS. This 9-month-old female lorikeet presented dead with no history of illness. The bird was found dead on exhibit. AIR SACCULITIS. This 12-year-old male tern was found down. The animal died despite treatment. At necropsy white foci were noted in the caudal air sacs.

SUSPECT HEAD TRAUMA HEMOSIDEROSIS. This approximately 37-year-old male flamingo died in the keeper’s arms once in the transport vehicle. The flock had been transferred to a new enclosure due to construction. The bird was presented alive for processing and had a deeply abraded bumble lesion. At necropsy the flamingo was in adequate body condition. The left pes had a medium bumble of the central pad that had a 5-8 mm. diameter gouge that bled antemortem. The gastrointestinal tract contained some digesta while ingesta was limited to sand in the ventriculus. The base of the tongue seemed quite thickened and edematous. The brain stem was surrounded by free dark blood and the deep calvaria was deeply ecchymotic. The brain was congested malacic and had free blood in the meninges. Sections of liver and small intestine were frozen for future use if needed.

LYMPHOMA AND LYMPHOID LEUKEMIA. This 5-year-old female chicken was found dead. The bird had no prior signs of illness and had recently been laying eggs at a normal rate. Necropsy revealed good body condition good hydration generalized vascular congestion thickened and opaque air sacs with adhesions to adjacent structures particularly the gastrointestinal and reproductive structures pale kidneys discolored ovary with degenerative and friable follicles.

EUTHANASIA CHRONIC NEPHRITIS GLOMERULOSCLEROSIS BRONCHIOLO-ALVEOLAR HYPERPLASIA SPINDLE CELL TUMOR. This 15-year-old male meerkat had an acute onset of disorientation and ataxia. The animal was humanely euthanized. At necropsy the lungs contained several masses. The liver was discolored tan.

SEVERE VASCULAR MINERALIZATION SEPTIC OOPHORITIS WITH MINERALIZATION MESANGIAL GLOMERULOPATHY. EUTHANASIA METASTATIC CARCINOMA GRANULOMATOUS STEATITIS. This 12-year-old female Amur tiger had a mammary adenocarcinoma diagnosed on 6/25/04 with removal of the left mammary chain and mammary mass. ARTERIOSCLEROSIS EUTHANASIA DEGENERATIVE CARDIOMYOPATHY/FIBROSIS. ISLET AMYLOIDOSIS BACTERIAL UROCYSTITIS WITH SEPSIS ANESTHETIC COMPLICATIONS. This 25-year-old macaque developed a sudden onset of depression. ENCEPHALOMALACIA SPINAL CORD HEMORRHAGE CHRONIC NEPHRITIS ENDOGENOUS LIPID PNEUMONIA. This 16-year-old male lion had a history of lameness and ataxia. BACTERIAL SEPTICEMIA WITH ABSCESS FORMATION. This 7.5-year-old male pitviper was found dead with no prior signs of illness. Necropsy revealed a perforated stomach and red intestines.

EMACIATION STRESS RUMINORETICULITIS ABOMASITIS AMYLOIDOSIS. This 7-year-old male Speke’s gazelle was found dead. It had been acting normal the previous day passing normal feces and urine. Only a small amount of liquid contents were in the rumen and the abomasal mucosa was congested. Multiple 0.5 cm. cystic structures were on the pancreas. The kidneys are small and firm with distinct corticomedullary junction. The bladder was filled with urine.

According to the history provided; this 9-year-old female alpaca was found down the evening of 10/15/17 and was taken to MSU VMC after failing to respond to treatment with banamine; baytril; ivermectin; and dexamethasone. On presentation at MSU; she was recumbent; unresponsive; hypothermic; tachycardic; and was breathing agonally. Ocular examination revealed an absent pupillary light response OS and positional nystagmus. Supportive treatment was unsuccessful; and she died on 10/17/17 and was submitted for necropsy and rabies testing the same day. An 87-kg female alpaca was necropsied 10/17/17. Autolysis was mild. An indwelling venous catheter was present in the right jugular vein. There was scant subcutaneous and visceral fat; and the animal had an overall body condition score of 3/9. The subcutaneous tissues over the mandible; inner thighs; and ventral abdomen were expanded by pale yellow gelatinous edema. There was red-tinged serous fluid in the peritoneum (300 mL) and thoracic cavity (80 mL). The pericardium contained approximately 5 mL of clear yellow thin fluid admixed with few white strands of fibrin. There were 10-15 0.3-0.5-cm irregular white foci in the left ventricular myocardium in the region of the aortic outflow tract. The lungs were mottled pink to dark red; wet; and oozed red serous fluid on cut section. Clusters of pinpoint to 1-mm diameter white round foci were scattered throughout the pleural surface of the right and left caudal lung lobes; consistent with endogenous lipid pneumonia. The cortex of the right kidney contained a focal 1-cm cyst. The jejunum contained dark red watery fluid digesta. There were formed fecal pellets in the colon. There were no other significant gross lesions. Body as a whole: Ventral subcutaneous edema Peritoneum; Thoracic cavity; Pericardium: Tricavitary effusion Lungs: Pulmonary edema; Multifocal subpleural lipogranulomas Kidney: Focal renal cortical cyst Open Comments: This alpaca had significant tricavitary effusion and edema for which the inciting cause was unclear. Such effusion and edema commonly form secondary to endoparasitism in alpacas and other small ruminants; however; no parasites were seen on gross examination. The endogenous lipid pneumonia and renal cyst are considered incidental findings in this case. Histopathologic examination of tissues and results will be released in a final report. Rabies testing results will be released in a separate report. Michelle Magagna; DVM Brain: rabies negative Comments: Histopathologic examination of tissues and additional diagnostic testing is pending. Results will be released in a final report. Michelle Magagna; DVM Representative sections of brain; trachea; lung; tongue; heart; thymus; spleen; liver; kidney; adrenal gland; pituitary gland; pancreas; thyroid gland; urinary bladder; skeletal muscle; esophagus; stomach; small intestine; and large intestine were examined. Autolysis was mild. The myocardium of the left ventricle contained multifocal locally extensive areas of myofiber necrosis and mineralization. Necrotic myofibers were characterized by hypereosinophilia; sarcolemmic clumping; loss of cross-striations; fragmentation; and nuclear pyknosis. Additionally within this region; there were occasional foci of fibrosis that variably separated and individualized myofibers. In sections of liver; the majority of centrilobular and midzonal hepatocytes contained a single large discrete lipid vacuole or multiple smaller lipid vacuoles; consistent with macro- and microvacuolar degeneration. Within the renal cortex; there were few focal aggregates of dilated tubules lined by attenuated cuboidal epithelium with increased cytoplasmic basophilia; consistent with tubular regeneration. Dilated tubules occasionally contained intraluminal eosinophilic proteinaceous fluid; and were variably surrounded by increased amounts of interstitial fibrosis. In one section; the renal cortex and medulla were regionally compressed by an expansile; well-demarcated cyst lined by flattened rectangular epithelial cells and surrounded by a thin fibrous capsule. Few tubules in the cortex and medulla were focally mineralized. In the lung; bronchiole-associated lymphoid tissue was multifocally mildly prominent and occasionally contained aggregates of foamy; vacuolated macrophages with intracytoplasmic brown; crystalline pigment. Few small aggregates of similar macrophages were scattered throughout the subpleural pulmonary interstitium. Alveolar septa were diffusely congested. Moderate numbers of eosinophils were scattered throughout the superficial and deep lamina propria of the small intestine. There were Heart; left ventricle: Multifocal myocardial necrosis; mineralization; and fibrosis Liver: Centrilobular to midzonal vacuolar degeneration Kidney: Multifocal tubular regeneration; Focal renal cyst; Mild multifocal tubular mineralization Lung: Mild BALT hyperplasia and pneumoconiosis Suspect nutritional cardiomyopathy Comments: The histologic lesions in the heart are most suggestive of a nutritional myopathy; such as is commonly seen with vitamin E/selenium deficiency. The grossly observed effusion and edema likely developed secondary to heart failure. The vacuolar degeneration in the liver was thought to represent hypoxic change resulting from terminal cardiac shock. The remainder of the lesions represent subclinical processes or incidental findings. Qualitative fecal analysis and liver vitamin E levels and trace mineral analysis are pending. Results will be reported as an addendum. Michelle Magagna; DVM Liver trace mineral analysis : Mildly elevated selenium (3.83 ug/g; reference interval 1-3 ug/g) Liver vitamin E levels: 316.18 ug/g Comments: While vitamin E and selenium appeared to be mildly elevated; these values are most suggestive of recent supplementation and likely do not reflect long-standing; established vitamin E/selenium levels in this alpaca. The histologic the histologic lesions in the heart remain consistent with white muscle disease; caused by vitamin E/selenium deficiency. This completes all diagnostic testing for this case. Michelle Magagna; DVM

INTESTINAL CONGESTION AND HEMORRHAGE FORESTOMACH GASTRITIS WITH INTRALESIONAL BACTERIA PROLIFERATIVE GLOMERULONEPHRITIS TUBULOINTERSTITIAL NEPHRITIS. SPLENIC HEMANGIOSARCOMA ADRENAL CARCINOMA HEMOABDOMEN. This 2-year-old male/castrated rat was found dead in the afternoon with no prior signs of illness. GASTROENTEROCOLITIS WITH HEMORRHAGE. This 1.5-year-old male rabbit was found dead with no prior signs of illness. No recent dietary changes or notable stressors had been noted. The cecum and portions of the colon were discolored dark red/purple and contained liquid fecal material. No formed fecal balls were observed. No other gross abnormalities were noted.

POSTANESTHETIC COMPLICATIONS CHRONIC HEPATOPATHY CARDIOPULMONARY SHOCK. This greater than 4-year-old female lorikeet was admitted to the hospital on 9/6 for seizure activity. The bird had improved the following day and was sedated for supportive care and ancillary procedures. The bird recovered well from anesthesia but was found dead two hours later. This bird had chronic poor plumage. Necropsy revealed lean to good body condition fractured feathers on both wings frayed feather tips fractured tail feathers and no other gross abnormalities.

This 5-year-old male alpaca presented to MSU VMC on 4/15/2015 for pain and labored breathing after being found lateral that morning. Physical exam indicated decreased lung sounds ventrally on the left side; no gut sounds; and a firm; bloated abdomen. Exploratory abdominal surgery revealed a large gas- and ingesta-filled C1 compartment of the stomach. Excessive ingesta was removed surgically. Postoperatively; the animal's condition deteriorated; with the development of significant bilateral pleural effusion and diarrhea. The animal died on the evening of 4/15; and was submitted for necropsy on 4/17. Additional history is on file at DCPAH. An 81-kg male alpaca was examined on 4/17/2015. Autolysis was moderate. The animal had adequate subcutaneous and visceral fat stores and an overall body condition of 5/9. There were bilateral chest tubes and nasal cannulas. A closed ventral midline abdominal surgical incision extended 13 cm cranial and 7 cm caudal to the umbilicus. There was 1L of watery; translucent; serosanguineous fluid in the abdominal cavity that had a urine-like smell; but the urogenital tract was intact. The thoracic cavity contained 500 mL of similar fluid with strands of free-floating fibrin. There were multifocal; random; pinpoint to 5-mm diameter petechiae and ecchymoses on the parietal pleura; visceral pleura; and epicardial surface along the coronary groove and the interventricular septum. The C1 compartment of the stomach was gas distended and had a 10-cm; linear; closed surgical incision along the left ventrolateral wall. The mucosal surface of C3 had numerous 2- to 5-mm diameter; white to tan; firm nodules and multifocal random petechia and ecchymoses; of which the largest measured 1 cm in diameter. The liver had an enhanced lobular pattern; and multiple (approximately 10) white to tan; firm nodules were multifocally randomly scattered throughout the liver parenchyma. The mucosal surface of the larynx was diffusely dark red. The esophagus contained a green to brown; 10-cm long; fairly formed but moist; dark green brown trichobezoar at the level of the tracheal carina. The esophageal mucosa in this region was diffusely dark red. No other significant lesions were observed. Whole body: hydroabdomen and hydrothorax/pleuritis; multifocal pleural and epicardial hemorrhages C3 stomach: multifocal mucosal nodules liver: multifocal nodules esophagus: trichobezoar; with associated mucosal hyperemia and hemorrhage Comments The hemorrhages and pleuritis are suggestive of septicemia. The noted firm nodules in the C3 stomach and liver are likely due to parasites. A final report is pending complete histologic evaluation; fecal parasite analysis; and aerobic culture of the liver and lungs. Erica Noland; DVM; MS Sections of brain; lung; trachea; thyroid gland; heart; spleen; liver; kidney; adrenal gland; stomach; intestine; and tongue are examined. There are multifocal; large organizing fibrin thrombi within hepatic; pulmonary; and esophageal blood vessels. In the liver; there is regionally extensive capsular and parenchymal fibrosis; with scattered multifocal hemorrhage. Thrombosed vessels are surrounded by variably dense rims of fibrosis. There are abundant intracytoplasmic accumulations of rhodanine- positive; coarse granular material within large numbers of primarily centrilobular to midzonal hepatocytes. There are multifocal centrilobular to random foci of hepatocellular necrosis admixed with small to moderate numbers of histiocytes containing rhodanine-positive granular material; lymphocytes; plasma cells; and fewer neutrophils. Perioportal and centrilobular regions are multifocally mildly expanded by similar cellular infiltrates. There is mild bile duct hyperplasia. The hepatic parenchyma is focally expanded by a region of mineralization associated with varying amounts of fibrosis and moderate numbers of macrophages. Similar foci of dystrophic mineralization are focally to multifocally present within the splenic parenchyma; the submucosa of C3; and the intestines; associated with various amounts of fibrosis and small to moderate numbers of macrophages. In the kidney; there are multifocal wedge-shaped areas of renal cortical coagulative necrosis characterized by hypereosinophilic tubular epithelial cells with fragmented nuclei (karyorrhexis). These regions are outlined peripherally by moderate congestion. Adjacent intact tubules multifocally contain bright eosinophilic proteinaceous material. The capsular surface is focally lined by plump reactive mesothelial cells and there are moderate aggregates of infiltrating lymphocytes. The lungs are mildly diffusely congested and alveolar spaces multifocally contain small numbers of histiocytes. The pleural surface is lined by Liver: Chronic fibrosing hepatitis; marked centrilobular to midzonal copper accumulation; mild bile duct hyperplasia; hepatic thrombosis; and multifocal dystrophic mineralization Kidney: Acute to peracute renal infarctions; multifocal tubular proteinosis; and lymphocytic serositis/peritonitis Lung: Focal pulmonary thrombus; mild alveolar histiocytosis; and pleural fibrosis Esophagus: Locally extensive transmural hemorrhage and edema Spleen/C3/Intestines: Multifocal dystrophic mineralization Chronic fibrosing hepatocellular necrosis and hepatitis; and multiorgan fibrin thrombi Comments The multifocal thrombosis is suggestive of disseminated intravascular coagulation; which may be related to chronic liver disease. The findings in the liver are both severe and chronic; and may be due to copper toxicosis; as suggested by excessive staining for copper in histologic sections. Quantification of the hepatic copper level is pending to confirm this; and an addendum report will be issued when results are available. The noted ischemic changes (i.e.; infarcts) in the kidney are likely due to thrombi not captured in the planes of sections examined. Thus; these renal lesions may also be associated with DIC. Effusions in both the thoracic and abdominal cavities may have been due to hypoproteinemia associated with liver disease; although total solids were apparently not low until after intravenous fluids administration. The multifocal dystrophic mineralization is consistent with old parasitic cysts. These foci are all similar in terms of chronicity--i.e.; similar degrees of fibrosis; mineralization; and mild macrophage infiltration; but with a lack of apparent parasites; suggesting the animal was treated for an infestation at one time. The locally extensive hemorrhage seen in the esophagus grossly and histologically was possibly associated with the trichobezoar identified at necropsy. Erica Noland; DVM; MS Copper-associated hepatitis Comments The quantitative copper amount of 525.05 ug/g dw in this case is consistent with copper toxicosis . A level this high is consistent with excessive dietary intake. Consultation with a veterinary nutritionist is recommended to address appropriate feeding for the remaining animals in the herd. There are several references to copper toxicosis in camelids in the published literature; including: Copper poisoning in four llamas. 1989. J Am Vet Med Assoc 195(7): 987-989. Erica Noland; DVM; MS

DEGENERATIVE CARDIAC DISEASE. This 28-year-old male California sea lion had chronic ocular problems but was otherwise healthy. It was found dead. Necropsy revealed a possible thyroid cyst thin walled right ventricle enlarged liver hyperemic stomach and petechiae in the pancreas.

Kidney: Moderate membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis; nonsuppurative interstitial nephritis with fibrosis Adrenal gland: Severe cortical hyperplasia Lung: Anthracosis Heart: Mild multifocal myocardial degeneration and fibrosis Liver: Moderate diffuse hepatic lipidosis Comment: A specific cause of death was not apparent upon histologic evaluation of the tissues. DEGENERATIVE CARDIOMYOPATHY VASCULOPATHY TRAUMA. This 7.5-year-old scarlet ibis was found dead. Necropsy revealed a large amount of intracoelomic fat rounded liver and subjectively thickened left ventricle.

PAPILLARY NECROSIS BRONCHOPNEUMONIA EUTHANASIA LUMPY JAW. This greater than 6-year-old female Parma wallaby was anesthetized on March 3rd to examine for lumpy jaw and during the procedure the animal developed cardiac arrest twice but was revived. The animal never regained normal mental function and although reflexes were intact the wallaby did not have voluntary motor control. Auscultation of the lungs revealed rales. Suspected pulmonary edema and contusions from resuscitation attempts were considered the likely cause for the rales. Supportive care was administered over the period of one week but the wallaby did not improve and euthanasia was performed for humane and diagnostic purposes. Necropsy revealed an area of thickened hard bone midway along the right mandible dark brown left thoracic wall with gelatinous texture possible thickening of the left ventricle of the heart dark red/purple lung lobes 3 mm. white raised lesion on the mucosal surface of the stomach and several areas of reddening throughout the intestinal tract.

Necropsy revealed moderate edema in the coelomic cavity and hind legs distended gastrointestinal tract and no other abnormalities.

EUTHANASIA CARDIOMYOPATHY FAT ATROPHY TRAUMA. This 22-year/7-month-old female colobus was humanely euthanized. It sustained wounds from a fight in the enclosure. Supportive care was initiated. There was a small amount of hemorrhage over the left jugular vein. There was 5 cc. of clear fluid in the pericardium. The spleen was 2 x 2.5 cm. in diameter and appeared very small. There was unclotted dark blood around the spinal cord. There was subdural hemorrhage. The brain appeared wet on cut section. There was subcutaneous edema in the ventral abdomen. There was about 40 cc. of golden tinged serosanguineous fluid in the abdomen.
